newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel bars Clal-Koor natural gas joint venture.
newsitem.headline: Israel bars Clal-Koor natural gas joint venture.

text.p: Clal Israel has not yet decided whether it will fight a decision by Israeli anti-trust authorities barring a natural gas consortium with Koor Industries, a spokesman said on Monday.
"We are studying the decision. We only received it yesterday," the Clal spokesman said. Regarding a possible court appeal, he said, "We haven't made up our mind yet."
A Koor spokesman declined to comment on the matter.

Meanwhile, sources at Clal and in the government denied there were hints in the decision that the anti-trust authorities would take a harder line on co-operation between Clal and the IDB group. "It concerns only the consortium," one source said.

David Tadmor, the commissioner for restrictive business practices, said on Sunday he would not exempt Middle East Energy (MEE) from anti-trust laws. MEE was formed by Koor, Clal and other partners to bid for a monopoly the Israeli government plans to award by tender for the import and distribution of natural gas.
"This consortium comprises two of the biggest conglomerates in the economy -- Koor and the IDB-Clal Group," Tadmor wrote.

"The joining of these forces...reduces competition between the two concerns and, in light of the high level of concentration in the Israeli economy, is likely to have a significant impact in connection with the natural gas tenders to be published."

The decision hinted that Tadmor would take a tougher line in cooperation between Clal and IDB Development Corp, which became Clal's single biggest shareholder last October after acquiring a block of shares from Bank Hapoalim.
"The de facto merger between IDB and Clal...puts in a problematic light any joint undertakings, particularly new undertakings by Koor and by IDB-Clal," he wrote.
However, a government source said Tadmor's decision referred only to MEE.
MEE's other partners include Mashab, the Dankner Group and Israel Petrochemical Industries. It was formed to compete in the tender to import and distribute natural gas.
Tadmor said he opposed any waiver for MEE because among other things its partners control other energy companies and because companies controlled by them would also be among MEE's biggest customers.
